cards.title: Why Transformers Replaced Everything
cards.content:
Before Transformers (2017), sequence modeling meant RNNs/LSTMs:
- Sequential processing — can't parallelize
- Long-range dependencies fade (even with LSTM gates)
- Training is slow ($O(n)$ sequential steps)

**Transformers solve all three** with **self-attention:**
- Fully parallel — every token attends to every other token simultaneously
- Direct connections between any two positions (no vanishing gradients over distance)
- Training is $O(1)$ depth (but $O(n^2)$ in sequence length)

The paper: *"Attention Is All You Need"* (Vaswani et al., 2017). The architecture has two parts: **encoder** (processes input) and **decoder** (generates output). Modern LLMs (GPT, LLaMA) use **decoder-only** Transformers.

cards.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
cards.content:
The core operation of every Transformer:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

- **Q** (Query): What am I looking for? $(n, d_k)$
- **K** (Key): What do I contain? $(n, d_k)$
- **V** (Value): What information do I provide? $(n, d_v)$

**Step by step:**
1. Compute attention scores: $QK^T$ → $(n, n)$ matrix
2. Scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$ — prevents softmax saturation for large $d_k$
3. Apply softmax row-wise — each row sums to 1
4. Multiply by V — weighted sum of values

**Why scale?** Without scaling, dot products grow as $O(d_k)$, pushing softmax into saturation (near one-hot). Scaling keeps gradients healthy.

cards.title: Multi-Head Attention
cards.content:
Instead of one attention function, use $h$ parallel "heads":

$$\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,...,\text{head}_h)W^O$$
$$\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)$$

With $d_{\text{model}} = 768$ and $h = 12$ heads: each head uses $d_k = d_v = 768/12 = 64$.

```python
def multihead_attention(Q, K, V, W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, n_heads):
    B, n, d = Q.shape
    dk = d // n_heads
    
    q = (Q @ W_q).reshape(B, n, n_heads, dk).transpose(0,2,1,3)
    k = (K @ W_k).reshape(B, n, n_heads, dk).transpose(0,2,1,3)
    v = (V @ W_v).reshape(B, n, n_heads, dk).transpose(0,2,1,3)
    
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2,-1)) / np.sqrt(dk)
    attn = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    out = (attn @ v).transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(B, n, d)
    return out @ W_o
```

**Why multiple heads?** Each head can attend to different aspects: syntax, semantics, positional patterns.

cards.title: The Causal Mask
cards.content:
For **autoregressive** generation (GPT-style), token $i$ must NOT attend to future tokens $j > i$.

Solution: **causal mask** — set future positions to $-\infty$ before softmax:

```python
def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    
    # Causal mask: upper triangle = -inf
    n = scores.shape[-1]
    mask = np.triu(np.ones((n, n)), k=1) * -1e9
    scores += mask
    
    attn = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return attn @ V
```

After softmax, masked positions become 0 — no information flows from the future.

**Interview favorite:** "Write causal self-attention from scratch." Know this cold: QKV projections, scaling, masking with `-inf`, softmax, multiply by V.

cards.title: Transformer Block: The Full Picture
cards.content:
Each Transformer block has two sub-layers:

**1. Multi-Head Self-Attention + Residual + LayerNorm**
$$\mathbf{x}' = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x} + \text{MHA}(\mathbf{x}))$$

**2. Feed-Forward Network + Residual + LayerNorm**
$$\mathbf{x}'' = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}' + \text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}'))$$

Where FFN is a simple 2-layer MLP:
$$\text{FFN}(x) = W_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2$$

$W_1$ projects up to $4d$ (the "expansion ratio"), $W_2$ projects back to $d$.

**Residual connections** are essential — they allow gradients to flow directly through the network (skip connections). Without them, deep Transformers can't train.

**LayerNorm** stabilizes training by normalizing activations across the feature dimension.

cards.title: Positional Encoding
cards.content:
Self-attention is **permutation-invariant** — it doesn't know token order! We add positional information.

**Original (sinusoidal):**
$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d})$$
$$PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d})$$

**Why sines/cosines?** For any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ — the model can learn relative positions.

**Modern alternatives:**
- **Learned positional embeddings** (BERT, GPT-2): just a lookup table. Simple and effective.
- **RoPE** (LLaMA, modern LLMs): Rotary position embeddings that encode relative positions directly in the attention computation. Now the standard.
- **ALiBi** (BLOOM): Adds linear biases to attention scores based on distance. No learned parameters.

cards.title: Transformer Interview Essentials
cards.content:
**Q: Computational complexity of self-attention?**
$O(n^2 d)$ — quadratic in sequence length. This is why context windows are expensive.

**Q: Encoder-only vs. Decoder-only vs. Encoder-Decoder?**
- Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional attention, good for understanding tasks
- Decoder-only (GPT): causal attention, good for generation
- Encoder-Decoder (T5, original Transformer): for seq2seq tasks

**Q: What does each attention head learn?**
Different heads capture: syntax (subject-verb), coreference (pronoun resolution), positional patterns (nearby tokens), semantic similarity.

**Q: Why does FFN have a 4x expansion?**
More parameters in a simple structure. The FFN acts as a key-value memory: $W_1$ acts as keys, $W_2$ as values. Most of the Transformer's parameters are in FFN layers.

**Q: Pre-norm vs. Post-norm?**
Pre-norm (LN before attention/FFN) is now standard — more stable training for deep models. Post-norm (original paper) needs careful LR warmup.

cards.title: Self-Attention vs. Cross-Attention
cards.content:
**Self-attention:** Q, K, V all come from the same sequence.
Used in: every Transformer layer for encoding context.

**Cross-attention:** Q comes from one sequence, K and V from another.
Used in: encoder-decoder models (decoder queries attend to encoder keys/values).

```python
# Self-attention
Q = X @ W_q  # X is the same for Q, K, V
K = X @ W_k
V = X @ W_v

# Cross-attention
Q = decoder_hidden @ W_q  # Q from decoder
K = encoder_output @ W_k   # K, V from encoder
V = encoder_output @ W_v
```

Cross-attention is how the decoder "looks at" the input. In machine translation, it's how the output language attends to the input language.

cards.title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
cards.content:
Standard Multi-Head Attention: each head has its own Q, K, V projections.
With 32 heads → 32 K matrices, 32 V matrices in the KV-cache. **Expensive!**

**GQA** (used in LLaMA 2/3, Gemma, Mistral): group heads and share K, V projections.

Example: 32 query heads, 8 KV groups → each K,V is shared by 4 query heads.

```python
def gqa(Q, K, V, n_heads, n_kv_heads):
    # Q: (B, n_heads, seq, dk)
    # K, V: (B, n_kv_heads, seq, dk)
    group_size = n_heads // n_kv_heads
    
    # Repeat K, V for each head in the group
    K = K.repeat(1, group_size, 1, 1)  # PyTorch
    V = V.repeat(1, group_size, 1, 1)
    
    scores = (Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1)) / sqrt(dk)
    return softmax(scores) @ V
```

**Why?** Reduces KV-cache memory by $n_{\text{heads}}/n_{\text{kv}}$ with minimal quality loss.

cards.title: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
cards.content:
**MQA** is the extreme case: ALL heads share ONE K and ONE V.

$n_{\text{kv\_heads}} = 1$

**Tradeoff:**
- MHA: Best quality, largest KV-cache
- GQA: Near-MHA quality, smaller KV-cache
- MQA: Fastest inference, smallest KV-cache, slight quality drop

| Variant | KV-cache size | Quality |
| MHA | $2 \times n_h \times d_k$ per token | Best |
| GQA | $2 \times n_{kv} \times d_k$ per token | Near-MHA |
| MQA | $2 \times d_k$ per token | Good |

**Industry adoption:**
- GPT-3: MHA
- PaLM: MQA
- LLaMA 2 (70B): GQA with 8 KV heads
- LLaMA 3: GQA (all sizes)
- Mistral: GQA

GQA has become the sweet spot for production LLMs.

cards.title: FlashAttention
cards.content:
Standard attention materializes the full $n \times n$ attention matrix → $O(n^2)$ memory.

**FlashAttention** computes exact attention without materializing the full matrix, using **tiling and kernel fusion:**

1. Split Q, K, V into blocks that fit in SRAM (fast GPU memory)
2. Compute attention one block at a time
3. Accumulate results using the **online softmax trick** (track running max and sum)
4. Never write the $n \times n$ matrix to HBM (slow GPU memory)

**Results:**
- Memory: $O(n)$ instead of $O(n^2)$
- Speed: 2-4x faster (fewer HBM reads/writes)
- Exact (not approximate!) — same output as standard attention

**Key insight:** The bottleneck is memory bandwidth (HBM ↔ SRAM), not compute. FlashAttention is **IO-aware** — it minimizes data movement.

Every modern LLM training framework uses FlashAttention. It's the single most important systems optimization for Transformers.

cards.title: Sliding Window & Sparse Attention
cards.content:
Full attention is $O(n^2)$. For very long sequences, we need subquadratic alternatives:

**Sliding Window Attention** (Mistral, Longformer):
Each token attends only to the $w$ nearest tokens. $O(nw)$ complexity.
Combined with multiple layers, information can still propagate across the full sequence.

**Sparse Attention** (BigBird, Longformer):
Combine local windowed attention + global tokens + random attention.

**Linear Attention** (Mamba, RWKV):
Replace softmax attention with linear operators → $O(n)$ complexity.
Mamba uses **selective state spaces**: a learned recurrence that decides what to remember/forget.

**Interview comparison:**
- Full attention: $O(n^2)$, best quality, standard for $n < 8K$
- Sliding window: $O(nw)$, simple, good for long contexts
- Linear/SSM: $O(n)$, emerging, trades some quality for speed

**Flash + Sliding Window** is the current production sweet spot (Mistral uses this).

cards.title: Attention Interview Lightning Round
cards.content:
**Q: Why Q, K, V instead of just similarity between embeddings?**
Separate projections let the model learn *what to look for* (Q), *what to advertise* (K), and *what to provide* (V) independently. A token's key and value serve different purposes.

**Q: What is the attention output for a single head?**
A weighted average of value vectors, where weights come from query-key similarity. Each output position is a different weighted combination of all input positions.

**Q: Can attention weights be negative?**
No — softmax outputs are in $(0, 1)$. But the resulting output can be negative (V can have negative entries).

**Q: What happens if we remove scaling $\sqrt{d_k}$?**
For large $d_k$, dot products become large, softmax becomes near-one-hot. Gradients vanish for all but the top-scoring key. Training becomes unstable.

**Q: How much memory does the KV-cache use?**
Per token: $2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv\_heads}} \times d_k \times \text{bytes}$. For LLaMA-70B with 4K context: ~1.2GB in fp16.

cards.title: RMSNorm — Simpler, Faster LayerNorm
cards.content:
**LayerNorm** normalizes by mean AND variance:
$$\text{LN}(x) = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta$$

**RMSNorm** drops the mean centering — just normalizes by RMS:
$$\text{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum x_i^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma$$

```python
def rmsnorm(x, weight, eps=1e-6):
    rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + eps)
    return (x / rms) * weight
```

**Why RMSNorm?**
- ~10-15% faster (no mean computation)
- Empirically matches LayerNorm quality
- Used in LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma — all modern LLMs
- Fewer parameters (no $\beta$ bias term)

**Pre-RMSNorm** (applying norm BEFORE attention/FFN) is now the standard — it's more stable than post-norm for deep models.**

cards.title: RoPE — Rotary Position Embeddings
cards.content:
Instead of ADDING positional info to embeddings, **RoPE** encodes position by ROTATING query and key vectors:

$$f(\mathbf{q}, m) = \mathbf{q} \cdot e^{im\theta}$$

In practice, it operates on pairs of dimensions:

```python
def apply_rope(x, freqs):
    # x: (..., d), freqs: (seq_len, d//2)
    x_pairs = x.reshape(*x.shape[:-1], -1, 2)
    x_complex = x_pairs[..., 0] + 1j * x_pairs[..., 1]
    x_rotated = x_complex * freqs
    return np.stack([x_rotated.real, x_rotated.imag], -1).reshape(x.shape)

def precompute_freqs(dim, seq_len, base=10000):
    freqs = 1.0 / (base ** (np.arange(0, dim, 2) / dim))
    t = np.arange(seq_len)
    angles = np.outer(t, freqs)
    return np.exp(1j * angles)
```

**Key property:** $\langle f(q,m), f(k,n) \rangle$ depends only on $m - n$ (relative position). This gives relative position encoding for free.**

cards.title: SwiGLU — The Modern Activation
cards.content:
The FFN in the original Transformer:
$$\text{FFN}(x) = W_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}(W_1 x)$$

**SwiGLU** replaces this with a gated activation:
$$\text{SwiGLU}(x) = W_2 \cdot (\text{Swish}(W_1 x) \odot W_3 x)$$

Where $\text{Swish}(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x)$ and $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication.

```python
def swiglu_ffn(x, W1, W3, W2):
    gate = x @ W1
    gate = gate * sigmoid(gate)  # Swish activation
    up = x @ W3
    return (gate * up) @ W2
```

**Note:** SwiGLU has 3 weight matrices instead of 2. To keep parameter count similar, the hidden dimension is $\frac{2}{3} \times 4d$ instead of $4d$.

**Why it works:** The gating mechanism ($W_3 x$) lets the network learn which features to pass through. Used in LLaMA, PaLM, Mistral.

cards.title: Weight Tying & Embedding Tricks
cards.content:
**Weight Tying:** Share the input embedding matrix with the output (LM head) projection.

If vocab size $V$ = 32K and $d$ = 4096:
- Input embedding: $(V, d)$ = 131M params
- Output projection: $(d, V)$ = 131M params

With tying: use the SAME matrix (transposed for output) → save 131M params.

```python
class LLM:
    def __init__(self, V, d):
        self.embed = np.random.randn(V, d) * 0.02
    
    def forward(self, token_ids):
        x = self.embed[token_ids]  # input embedding
        # ... transformer layers ...
        logits = x @ self.embed.T  # output projection (tied!)
        return logits
```

**Used in:** GPT-2, LLaMA, most modern LLMs.

**Other embedding tricks:**
- Rotary embeddings (RoPE) replace absolute position embeddings
- BPE tokenization (32K-128K vocab is standard)

cards.title: Putting It All Together: LLaMA Block
cards.content:
A modern LLM Transformer block (LLaMA-style):

```python
def llama_block(x, attn_w, ffn_w, norm_w):
    # Pre-norm + GQA attention + residual
    h = rmsnorm(x, norm_w['attn'])
    h = gqa_attention(h, attn_w)  # with RoPE
    x = x + h  # residual
    
    # Pre-norm + SwiGLU FFN + residual
    h = rmsnorm(x, norm_w['ffn'])
    h = swiglu_ffn(h, ffn_w['W1'], ffn_w['W3'], ffn_w['W2'])
    x = x + h  # residual
    
    return x
```

**Full LLaMA architecture:**
1. Token embedding (+ RoPE applied in attention)
2. N × LLaMA blocks
3. Final RMSNorm
4. Linear head (tied with embedding)

**vs. Original Transformer:**
- RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm
- Pre-norm instead of post-norm
- SwiGLU instead of ReLU FFN
- RoPE instead of sinusoidal/learned positions
- GQA instead of MHA
- No bias terms anywhere

cards.title: Building Blocks Interview Essentials
cards.content:
**Q: Pre-norm vs post-norm — why does it matter?**
Pre-norm: gradients pass through residual path unscaled → stable training without careful LR warmup. Post-norm can diverge for deep models.

**Q: Why no bias terms in modern LLMs?**
PaLM showed removing biases doesn't hurt quality but enables tensor parallelism optimizations. Simplicity + efficiency.

**Q: What's the memory footprint of a 7B parameter model?**
fp32: 28GB. fp16: 14GB. int8: 7GB. int4: 3.5GB. Plus KV-cache during inference.

**Q: RoPE base frequency — what happens if you change it?**
Higher base = longer effective context window but weaker short-range position signal. LLaMA 3 uses base=500K for 128K context (vs. 10K for 8K context in LLaMA 2).

**Q: Why is the FFN hidden dim $\frac{8}{3}d$ in LLaMA?**
SwiGLU has 3 matrices. $\frac{8}{3}d \times 3 = 8d$ total params ≈ the $4d \times 2 = 8d$ params in a standard ReLU FFN.

cards.title: The Fine-Tuning Problem
cards.content:
You want to adapt a 7B-parameter LLM to your task. **Full fine-tuning** means updating ALL 7B parameters:
- Need 28GB+ GPU memory just for weights (fp32)
- Plus optimizer states (Adam: 2x weights = 56GB more)
- Plus gradients and activations
- Total: **~120GB+ for a 7B model**

This is expensive and stores a full copy per task.

**Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)** freezes the base model and only trains a small number of new parameters:
- LoRA: ~0.1-1% of original parameters
- Only 10-100MB of new weights per task
- Can merge into base model for zero inference overhead

This is the dominant approach for adapting LLMs today.

cards.title: LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation
cards.content:
**Core idea:** Weight updates during fine-tuning have low rank. So instead of updating a full $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, learn a low-rank decomposition:

$$W' = W + \Delta W = W + BA$$

Where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, and $r \ll \min(d, k)$.

```python
class LoRALinear:
    def __init__(self, W_frozen, r=8, alpha=16):
        d, k = W_frozen.shape
        self.W = W_frozen  # frozen
        self.A = np.random.randn(r, k) * 0.01
        self.B = np.zeros((d, r))
        self.scale = alpha / r
    
    def forward(self, x):
        base = x @ self.W.T
        lora = x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T * self.scale
        return base + lora
```

**Initialization:** $A \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, $B = 0$. This means $\Delta W = 0$ at start — training begins from the pre-trained model exactly.

cards.title: LoRA Hyperparameters
cards.content:
**Rank $r$:** Controls capacity of the update.
- $r = 8$: Typical default. Works well for most tasks.
- $r = 16-64$: For complex tasks or larger models.
- Higher $r$ = more parameters, more expressive, slower.

**Scaling factor $\alpha/r$:** Controls the magnitude of LoRA updates.
- $\alpha = 2r$ is common (so scale = 2)
- Higher $\alpha$ → larger updates → faster adaptation but less stable

**Which layers to adapt?**
- Original paper: Q and V projections only
- Practice: all linear layers (Q, K, V, O, FFN) works best
- Applying LoRA to just attention: good. To everything: better.

**Parameter count for $r=8$ on a 7B model:**
Each linear layer adds $2 \times r \times d$ params. ~20M total ≈ 0.3% of 7B.

**Merging for inference:**
$$W_{\text{merged}} = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA$$
No extra latency at inference time — just add the LoRA weights to the base model once.

cards.title: QLoRA — Quantized LoRA
cards.content:
**QLoRA** makes fine-tuning even cheaper:
1. Quantize the base model to **4-bit** (NF4 data type)
2. Add LoRA adapters in fp16/bf16
3. Train ONLY the LoRA parameters

**Key innovations:**
- **NF4 (NormalFloat4):** Optimal 4-bit quantization for normally distributed weights
- **Double quantization:** Quantize the quantization constants too
- **Paged optimizers:** Use CPU RAM for optimizer states that don't fit in GPU

**Result:** Fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU.

Memory breakdown for 7B with QLoRA:
- Base model (4-bit): ~3.5GB
- LoRA params (bf16): ~20MB
- Optimizer states: ~40MB
- Activations: varies
- **Total: ~8-12GB** (vs. 120GB for full fine-tuning!)

QLoRA quality matches full fine-tuning in most benchmarks.

cards.title: Other PEFT Methods
cards.content:
**Prefix Tuning:** Prepend learned "soft tokens" to the input at every layer.
- Tokens are virtual (not in vocab)
- 0.1% of parameters
- Less expressive than LoRA

**Adapters:** Insert small trainable layers between frozen Transformer blocks.
- bottleneck architecture: project down → ReLU → project up
- Adds inference latency (can't merge)

**IA3 (Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying):**
- Learn per-element scaling vectors for K, V, and FFN
- Even fewer parameters than LoRA
- Very fast training

**DoRA (Weight-Decomposed LoRA):**
- Decomposes weight into magnitude and direction
- Applies LoRA only to direction
- Closer to full fine-tuning behavior

**Current best practice:** LoRA or QLoRA with $r=16$, applied to all linear layers. It's simple, efficient, and works.

cards.title: LoRA Interview Essentials
cards.content:
**Q: Why does LoRA work? Why are updates low-rank?**
Pre-trained models are already close to the task solution. Fine-tuning makes small adjustments in a low-dimensional subspace. The "intrinsic dimensionality" of the update is much smaller than the full parameter space.

**Q: Can you stack multiple LoRA adapters?**
Yes. Keep base model frozen, swap LoRA weights for different tasks. This is how you serve one base model for many users cheaply.

**Q: LoRA vs. full fine-tuning — when is full FT better?**
When the task is very different from pre-training (e.g., new language), or you need maximum quality and have the compute budget.

**Q: What's catastrophic forgetting? Does LoRA help?**
Full fine-tuning can "forget" pre-training knowledge. LoRA mitigates this because the base weights are frozen — you can always remove the adapter to recover the original model.

**Q: LoRA for inference — any overhead?**
Zero, after merging: $W_{\text{new}} = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$. The merged model is architecturally identical to the original.

cards.title: Why LLM Inference is Hard
cards.content:
LLM inference has two phases:

**1. Prefill (prompt processing):**
Process all input tokens in parallel. Compute-bound. Fast.

**2. Decode (token generation):**
Generate one token at a time, autoregressively. **Memory-bandwidth-bound.** Slow.

Each generated token requires:
- Loading ALL model weights from memory
- Attending to ALL previous tokens (growing KV-cache)
- For one output token

**The math:** A 7B model in fp16 = 14GB. At 2TB/s bandwidth (A100), reading weights takes ~7ms per token → ~140 tokens/sec max. Most of the GPU's compute is idle!

This is the **memory wall** — and why inference optimization is critical for production LLMs.

cards.title: KV-Cache — The Core Optimization
cards.content:
During autoregressive decoding, the K and V matrices for previous tokens don't change. **Cache them!**

```python
def generate_with_kv_cache(model, prompt_ids, max_tokens):
    kv_cache = {}  # layer -> (K, V)
    
    # Prefill: process all prompt tokens
    logits, kv_cache = model.forward(
        prompt_ids, kv_cache=None
    )
    
    for _ in range(max_tokens):
        next_token = sample(logits[:, -1])
        # Decode: only process the NEW token
        logits, kv_cache = model.forward(
            [next_token], kv_cache=kv_cache
        )
        # kv_cache grows by 1 position per step
```

**Without KV-cache:** Each new token recomputes attention over all previous tokens → $O(n^2)$ total work for $n$ tokens.

**With KV-cache:** Each new token only computes its own Q, concatenates to cached K,V → $O(n)$ per token, $O(n^2)$ total.

**KV-cache memory for LLaMA-70B, 4K context, fp16:**
80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 4096 tokens × 2 bytes × 2 (K+V) = ~1.3GB

cards.title: Quantization — Making Models Smaller
cards.content:
Reduce precision of weights (and optionally activations):

**Common formats:**
- fp32 → fp16/bf16: 2x compression, minimal quality loss
- fp16 → int8: 2x compression, <1% quality loss
- fp16 → int4: 4x compression, 1-3% quality loss

**Popular methods:**

**GPTQ:** Post-training quantization using second-order info (Hessian). Quantizes layer by layer, compensating for each layer's error.

**AWQ (Activation-Aware):** Not all weights are equally important. Protect the 1% of weights that correspond to large activations.

**GGUF/GGML (llama.cpp):** CPU-friendly quantization. Various formats: Q4_0, Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M.

**Rule of thumb for quality:**
- Q8 (int8): Nearly lossless
- Q6_K: Very good
- Q4_K_M: Good tradeoff (most popular)
- Q4_0: Noticeable degradation
- Q2: Significant quality loss

cards.title: PagedAttention & vLLM
cards.content:
**Problem:** KV-cache memory must be pre-allocated per request. Different sequences have different lengths → massive memory waste.

Example: Reserve 2K tokens of KV-cache per request, but average usage is 500 tokens → 75% wasted.

**PagedAttention** (vLLM) applies OS virtual memory concepts:
- Divide KV-cache into fixed-size **pages** (e.g., 16 tokens each)
- Allocate pages on demand, not upfront
- Pages can be non-contiguous in physical memory
- Share pages across requests (for common prefixes)

**Results:**
- 2-4x higher throughput vs. naive serving
- Near-zero memory waste
- Efficient prefix caching (important for system prompts)

**vLLM** implements PagedAttention and is the de facto standard for LLM serving.

**Continuous batching:** Don't wait for all sequences to finish. As one completes, immediately start another. Keeps GPU utilization high.

cards.title: Speculative Decoding
cards.content:
**Idea:** Use a small, fast **draft model** to generate $K$ candidate tokens, then verify them in parallel with the large model.

```
1. Draft model generates K=5 tokens quickly
2. Large model processes all 5 in ONE forward pass
3. Accept tokens where large model agrees
4. Reject and resample from the first disagreement
```

**Why it works:** Most tokens are "easy" (the draft model gets them right). Only hard tokens need the large model's full power.

**Typical speedup:** 2-3x for code/structured text (high acceptance), 1.3-1.5x for creative text (lower acceptance).

**Key property:** The output distribution is EXACTLY the same as the large model alone. It's mathematically lossless — just faster.

**Variants:**
- Medusa: Multiple prediction heads on the SAME model (no draft model needed)
- Self-speculative: Use early-exit layers of the same model as draft
- EAGLE: Learns a lightweight draft head

cards.title: Inference Interview Essentials
cards.content:
**Q: Why is LLM inference memory-bound during decode?**
Each token loads the full model weights (~14GB for 7B) but does very little compute (one token × model). The arithmetic intensity is too low to saturate the GPU's compute units.

**Q: How does batching help?**
Multiple sequences share the weight-loading cost. Processing 32 tokens (one per sequence) with one weight load is 32x better arithmetic intensity.

**Q: What is the KV-cache memory for a model with $L$ layers, $h$ KV-heads, $d_k$ head dim, sequence length $n$?**
$2 \times L \times h \times d_k \times n \times \text{bytes\_per\_element}$

**Q: FP8 vs INT8 quantization?**
FP8 (E4M3) keeps a wider dynamic range. INT8 needs calibration data. FP8 is becoming standard on H100 GPUs.

**Q: What's tensor parallelism vs. pipeline parallelism?**
Tensor: split each layer across GPUs. Pipeline: assign different layers to different GPUs. Tensor is better for latency, pipeline for throughput.
